speechtext: Madam Speaker, I want to ask my hon. colleagues to condemn the actions of the Quebec Government which are now causing another border dispute between New Brunswick and Quebec. Madam Speaker, we all know that the construction regulations prevent manpower mobility within Quebec and Canada. I would invite my hon. colleagues to vigorously censure this attitude which deprives Quebec workers of mobility within their own province and workers across Canada from having access to the labour market in Quebec.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER INCLUDE EMPLOYMENT MEASURES IN BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, instead of necessarily condemning the Government of Quebec, I want to take advantage of this opportunity to condemn the lack of adequate measures to create jobs across Canada, especially in my own province which is severely affected by the lack of such measures. Unfortunately, we are experiencing record unemployment and record bankruptcies, and since we will have time for some serious reflexion during the Easter holidays, I would urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to give some serious thought to proposals for effective job creation in his next budget. The Minister of Finance keeps saying to anyone who will listen that economic recovery is just around the corner, but we know perfectly well that in 1984, we will still have to support from 1,500,000 to two million unemployed workers. In the circumstances, I think the Minister of Finance should stop making promises which are almost never kept and
start making some substantial proposals in his budget providing for genuine economic recovery and job creation, and take advantage of this opportunity to make a wise choice, all of which has been sadly lacking during the last fifteen years. That is my Easter message for the Minister of Finance, and I would ask him to give the situation some serious thought and to show some compassion for and an interest in what is happening to, our unemployed workers in Canada and especially in "la Belle province".

subsubtopic: A REMEMBRANCE OF UNITED NATIONS DELEGATE, ANDREI GROMYKO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is not my intention to raise a matter that is argument or debate, but I hope it is of interest. It so happens that in 1945 and 1946 I was among those who represented Canada at the first meetings of the United Nations. The other person with me was Gordon Graydon, a Conservative Member who served in this House for about 19 years. In the process we were quite interested in certain people there, especially Andrei Gromyko. Both Mr. Graydon and I found that we could have an interesting discussion with Mr. Gromyko, and in view of this we dared to hope he might be useful to our country in the future. He wrote me a letter which was dated April 25, 1946. This was after Mr. Graydon and I had returned to Ottawa. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Knowles:
It was great pleasure for me to receive your kind letter of April 16th, congratulating me in connection with my appointment as the Permanent Representative of the USSR to the Security Council of the United Nations Organization.
I am pleased to learn that you have visited Moscow and enjoyed your stay there. I hope that we shall have frequent opportunities of meeting each other in the future. It was kind of you to remind me of Mr. Gordon Graydon. Please convey my greetings to him.
With best personal wishes and warm regards,
Sincerely yours,
Andrei A. Gromyko
I think it is of interest. I hope it might just be.

March 30, 1983

I take this opportunity to explain as well the position of the Canadian Government. Canada abstained at the third committee because the committee refused to hear the Turkish-Cypriot member of the commission on the disappearance of Greek Cypriots. I should like to emphasize that Canada has the second largest peace-keeping force in Cyprus and that we contribute more than 20 per cent of the financial resources. Our financial contribution to peace-keeping in Cyprus exceeds all our other peace-keeping commitments throughout the world.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Liberal Cabinet recently passed an Order in Council placing the FN-FAL combat rifle on the restricted weapons list.
The Firearms Control Research Group states that there is only one case on record of this type of firearm being used illegally. Few criminals would use a bulky, expensive weapon like the FN-FAL in the commission of an offence. By and large, criminals use pistols because they are cheaper, lightweight, and easy to conceal. Few gun collectors will follow the Government modification guidelines accompanying the Order in Council designed to prevent the rifle from being adapted to machine gun capability because these guidelines may, and could, result in the rifles blowing up in their faces when they attempt to fire them.
This Government can put anything on the restricted weapons list through Order in Council, with no review in Parliament. This totally irresponsible use of Orders in Council is just a means to bypass the House of Commons, which has become a serious irritant of this arrogant Government.
There is justifiable fear among gun owners and collectors that the eventual end to firearms registration will be the confiscation of all firearms in Canada. These are responsible Canadians who are bona fide collectors, not criminals.
The FN-FAL meets none of the criteria generally applying to restricted weapons. There is little reason to register the FN-FAL rifle when a police authorized firearms acquisition certificate is already required to purchase one. This Order in Council is wasteful, unnecessary, expensive and must be reversed.

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATION ON BEHALF OF DIEPPE VETERANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last year was the fortieth anniversary of the Dieppe raid and at that time many hopes were expressed that changes would be made in the rules pertaining to compensation for former prisoners of war, changes which would recognize the unique situation in which Dieppe veterans find themselves, but no action has been forthcoming from the Government.
At present the 20 per cent compensation for Dieppe veterans does not take into account the special suffering endured by those captured at Dieppe who were tied, then chained, and finally made to go on a three-month dead march. As the national President of the Dieppe Veterans said before a Senate committee just lask week, the Dieppe veterans are fed up and are wondering whether the Government wants to do the same to them as it did to First World War veterans when it waited until most of them were dead before making them eligible for the war veterans allowance.
It is about time that the Government recognized the special claim that Dieppe veterans have on the Canadian public, not just because of their suffering but because of the importance of their sacrifice to the eventual successful landing on D-Day in June, 1944. In this respect may I also suggest that a campaign medal be struck for the Dieppe force. This, combined with improvements in the pension benefits available to them, would go a long way to meeting the long overdue need for the Canadian Government to recognize properly those who came back from that terrible morning on the beaches of Dieppe.
March 30, 1983

subtopic: GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO GROWTH IN UNEMPLOYMENT
GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO GROWTH IN UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1982 Canada had, on average, 1.3 million people officially unemployed. Today the official number of unemployed is 1.6 million. Unofficially, as every Canadian knows, the number of people who need jobs is well over two million. The Government's response to the growing crisis has been to make promises, stall, break promises, and wait for some evidence of recovery in the U.S., all the while warning Canadians that it is unable to do much to bring down unemployment.
Today the despair of construction workers, woodworkers and truckers over their inability to find work, has erupted into violence in New Brunswick. Workers in the steel industry in that Province find out that a mine closure will put another 550 people out of work. This Government, which came to office on a promise of revitalizing Canada's industrial capacity to be better able to create jobs, and which promised to be an active player rather than a passive referee in industrial development, has now killed the notion of an industrial strategy because it believes it cannot make it work.
The Government has abandoned another major plank in the campaign which brought it to office. It has acknowledged its total inability and unwillingness to deal with the most serious economic problem facing the country, which is the obscenely high level of unemployment.

We are told by the Minister that, apart from the band-aid treatment we get from his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, we have to wait for his budget. I would like to ask the Minister on behalf of the 824,000 longterm unemployed, those who have been unemployed for longer than three and a half months, when can we expect that budget?

Madam Speaker, on the other side of the ledger I was happy to see today in a report of the Conference Board a survey of business confidence

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a further question to the Minister of Finance. Madam Speaker, I would remind my hon. friend, first of all, that the Government has direct job programs in operation already which are worth $2 billion. Second, I invite him to wait for the measures contained in the budget. Third, I will tell him that I am flabbergasted that a Conservative takes the view that the private sector has no role to play in the growth of the economy. He said that business confidence will not put bread on the table of the unemployed. Surely, in the Canadian economy, the private sector is going to be the engine of growth in this country, and the private sector is going to create the jobs which we need for millions of Canadians at the present time. Those jobs are not going to be created by the Government. We are not trying to create more bureaucrats and more officials. We are trying to arrive at a situation where there would be more jobs for Canadians created predominantly by the private sector. The statement by the Hon. Member is a flabbergasting one.

Madam Speaker, we now know what the problem is. The Minister of Finance is constantly flabbergasted. That is why he cannot address the real problems of which I am talking. I am talking about the problems of those who are unemployed now. He knows that, before he can get the economy restored to full level, it will take at least three years to restore the jobs which have been lost.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration and follows from the Minister's affirmation that he is seeking to expand employment, which we are all seeking. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the sad story of Kelly Cook is known to thousands of Canadians. On April 22, 1981, this beautiful fifteen-year-old girl was abducted from her home in Standard, where she lived with her parents, Marion and Walter Cook, and her sister and brother; two and one half months later she was found murdered, bound with ropes and weighted down with cinder blocks in Chin Lake, in southern Alberta. ["Mr. Speaker, Canadians are very conscious of the alarming number of nuclear weapons presently in the hands of the superpowers. They dread the thought that they might one day be used, and ponder over the dangers inherent in the existence of such arsenals. We are all aware of the devastation that would result from a nuclear war. In the face of the uncertainty that exists, many groups and individuals in the West are calling for an end to the development and deployment of new weapons, judging the quantity already in existence to be ample. This applies to strategic weapons as well as the intermediate-range missiles in Europe. Is it possible to accept the status quo in these two areas, and does it make sense to do so?
The governments of the NATO countries have decided to deploy Pershing II rockets and Cruise missiles in Europe as of this year if sufficient progress is not made in negotiations concerning this category of weapons in the coming months. It would have been much easier, in the short term, to pretend that the gigantic armament effort being made by the Warsaw Pact nations, in both the conventional and nuclear areas, was only a figment of our imagination. That is what the European countries did in the thirties. The imbalance that already existed in 1979, when NATO saw the need to react to the massive deployment of Soviet SS-20 missiles, has now become even greater, because the U.S.S.R. has since almost doubled the number of these missiles. Our allies are being held under a constant threat of destruction by more than 350 of these missiles, for which the West has no equivalent.
Canada has always been an advocate of peace, justice and freedom, but it must honour its commitments. The North Atlantic Alliance, of which Canada is a founding member, was formed to avoid a recurrence of war in Europe. Our soldiers who gave their lives for the liberation of Europe must not be said to have died in vain.
The Canadian Government, in accord with the other members of NATO, is very much in favour of verifiable agreements that would limit and then reduce nuclear weapons stocks on both sides, hopefully leading to eventual elimination. However, such an objective can only be achieved if the West shows its determination not to remain indifferent in the face of what
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
might constitute a means of applying considerable pressure. History has demonstrated that it is impossible to bring about a substantial diminution of armaments when the forces of one side outweigh the other's, as is presently the case in Europe. What reason would the side with the greater forces have to destroy or to dismantle the weapons that give it its hard-earned advantage, when no similar reduction had to be made by the other? Aggression is fostered by a state of inequality and a lack of determination, with the appearance of weakness.
Our policy is not one of confrontation. On the contrary, it is the only way open to us in the slow process of nuclear arms limitation and disarmament. It is based on the concept of deterrence, which has given us a hitherto unequalled period of almost 40 years without a major conflict in this region of Europe where military forces of unprecedented size are facing each other. And this is where the real merit of mutual deterrence lies. There can be no recourse to atomic weapons, because the superpowers have the capacity to resist a preemptive strike and to inflict on the aggressor a degree of destruction that would obviate the political acceptability of initiating a strike. Nor has there been any use of conventional weapons, which over the two World Wars alone were responsible for tens of millions of deaths and so much destruction.
There were more victims in the bombardment of Tokyo on March 9, 1945 than at Hiroshima; 83,600 deaths and 102,000 wounded, compared with 80,000 deaths and 70,000 wounded at Hiroshima. That is no exoneration of the travesty that happened at Hiroshima. We all hope and pray that that will never be repeated. It will not be repeated if one side, the West, shows weakness in fight in the face of Soviet might. This is the result of the state of mutual deterrence that has gradually established itself between the superpowers and opposing alliances.
The strategy of non-war and non-use of forces can exist only in so far as the fragile equilibrium is maintained. There exists a moral obligation to keep intact the state of deterrence and to negotiate in good faith nuclear and conventional arms control agreements which are balanced and verifiable and which will reduce the arsenals of both sides to the lowest possible level. It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that both sides in this very important issue, this issue upon which the very survival of our world depends, will in fact be responsible, so that neither side will proceed to the development of any further new weapons, but will put all of their resources which they are now expending on the development of new weapons into the development of a means of peace, the development of a means of reduction of arms, and the development of the means to achieve a world where men and women and future generations can live without the fear of a nuclear holocaust and can have a reasonable hope that the world, as we know it, will survive. We will then be able to truly progress and leave the world a better place for future generations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Anguish (The Battlefords-Meadow Lake) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-678, an Act to declare Canada a Nuclear Weapons Free Zone, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the co-operation of all Members of the House this afternoon in having this Bill come forward for debate in Private Members' hour. I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) who agreed to defer his Bill in favour of mine. I would also like to thank the Hon. Member for Dauphin (Mr. Lewycky) who seconded the motion so that Bill C-678 could come before us this afternoon.
It is of paramount importance to debate Bill C-678 before the Easter break for a number of reasons. One is the possibility that the Cruise missile might be tested any day now over Canadian territory. This missile has been slated for testing in the area of the Cold Lake Air Force Base and into the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range, which is part of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency that I represent here in the House of Commons.
In addition, I am very concerned about one Karen Harrison who has been fasting in our galleries for a number of days. She has stated that she will not cease her fast until such time as this Bill is given debate in the House of Commons.
I would like to say, however, that I hope this debate is only a beginning to the nuclear question and not an end in itself. We have to continue addressing the nuclear weapons problem very seriously. Bill C-678 basically does two things. First, it would declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone. That would prevent the testing of the Cruise missile over Canadian territory. The Bill would go on from there to do a number of other things. This Bill would prevent the manufacture, use, importation and export of any nuclear weapons or weaponry on or over Canadian territory.
Second, the Bill puts forward the will of this Parliament and country for the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) to go to the United Nations and present a resolution calling for the United Nations to conduct a world referendum on nuclear disarmament. This opinion, I think, has been demonstrated in referenda in municipal elections across the country. There is a growing concern over nuclear weapons and the testing of nuclear weaponry over Canadian territory.
I have a local concern having to do with the testing of the Cruise missile in the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range. If the testing of the Cruise missile is granted within Canadian territory, the air launched Cruise missiles will be dropped over the Beaufort Sea from B-52 bombers and will cruise over the Northwest Territories, northern Alberta, into Saskatchewan in the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range. This local concern arises over the possibility of a Cruise missile landing in some area other than the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range. I know the Cruise missile does not have an explosive capability in the initial testing but I think that matters not for someone living in Beauval, Canoe Narrows, Meadow Lake, Pierceland
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
or Goodsoil if this Cruise missile were to land in someone's livingroom or somewhere in those communities. This is a real concern of the constituents of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake about the testing of the Cruise missile.
If this Bill were to pass with the consent of Members of Parliament here and go to committee, it would clear up that concern for a great many people in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency and for people in other areas who are concerned about the testing of the Cruise missile over Canadian territory.
In addition to that, I have a much more serious and global concern about the nuclear arms question. Many people do not see much hope for the future in face of the possibility of nuclear war. Regardless of what some people say, you would have very little chance of limiting a nuclear war once it began. People are concerned about the destructive capability of nuclear weaponry. The two superpowers have likely more parity in destructive capability than they have ever had at any time in our history, certainly since the nuclear arms race began and since the devastating effects of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki toward the end of the Second World War.
This is not a question of the different countries involved, be it the U.S.S.R., the U.S.A., Canada, or any other country in the world. It is not a political question about nuclear arms and about Canada becoming involved in the nuclear arms race, because it not only affects New Democrats, Progressive Conservatives and Liberals, but the Canadian community and beyond that the global community of this planet.
Canadians have been respected worldwide for a number of years, likely since Confederation, in terms of being a peacekeeping force in the world. We have, however, risen to arms during certain times in our history. Canadians have fought for the cause of this country and our freedom as well as for the preservation of democracy in other places around the world. I am sure in the face of pressing times and world confrontation that Canadians would rise to that call again. Canadians have always been viewed as peace-loving people, but a people that will fight for democracy. We are not aggressors but we do believe in the rights of individuals.
You have to have conventional armed forces, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately, there may still be a need for them because of other aggressive forces in the world. But that concern and need is very different from nuclear warfare or nuclear weaponry. It is not a matter of a young person fighting in a nuclear war. Conventional armed forces would have very little play in such an event. A nuclear war, once started, would be devastating for all people whether involved in military or in public life.
I believe we have to start looking for a way to gear down, to freeze, nuclear weapons and at some point eliminate nuclear weapons from the face of this earth. I know at this point in time that might seem very idealistic to many Canadians. It is not idealistic to me. It is something that we must seriously work toward if we want to preserve this planet, if not for our

March 30, 1983
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
own future, for the future of our children, our grandchildren and for the generations to come.
Canada has respect as a peacekeeper, and I think it is within the realm of possibility that Canada can play a role as a mediator between superpowers. We can start working toward serious arms reduction on the face of this planet, which has an economic cost which boggles the mind. If the amount spent on armaments throughout the world during a two-week period was spent on education, clothing, housing and medical needs, most of the poverty throughout the world would be eliminated. In many cases that poverty has caused some of the world conflicts which we have seen. It is that poverty and lack of equity throughout the world which has caused dissension among different races of people and within races of people themselves.
In order to maintain our credibility, we should not become involved in the nuclear arms race. If we want to seriously strive for a world free of nuclear arms, we must clean our own house before we advise others on how to solve the nuclear weapons issue.
I believe that the argument that we have a NATO obligation to test the Cruise missile over Canadian territory is somewhat false. There are other countries within NATO which disagree with the testing of the Cruise missile and the escalation of the arms race. I believe that Canada should be counted among those countries so that we may keep the respect and dignity which we need and deserve in international affairs.
There is nothing in writing which obliges Canada to test nuclear weapons on or over our territory. I hope that this Bill will pass through Parliament during Private Members' Business today so that it can go to committee where Parliamentarians can begin seriously to address the nuclear weapons issue.
There are presently 32 NDP Members of Parliament in Canada. We are united and have the total support of the NDP caucus for having Canada declared a nuclear weapons free zone and to work seriously toward nuclear disarmament throughout the world.
Since I believe this is largely a non-partisan issue, I wish to point out that there are Members from the Liberal Party and Members from the Conservative Party who support the concept of which I speak today. I do not wish to alienate those Members but have them join us in an agreement that can give Canada the self-respect and international respect that we need to meaningfully work toward having a world free of nuclear arms.
I would point out to the people of Canada that they can play a very important role in this process. Since Canadians have access to their elected officials, I would urge all Canadians who are listening to this debate, watching it on television or who will read it in Hansard, to go to their Member of Parliament or provincial member of the legislature, and to their municipal councillors, aldermen and mayors, to ask them to take a stand on the nuclear weapons issue.
With respect to Members of Parliament in particular, I think constituents should be buttonholding their MPs to make them stand up and call for a country that is a nuclear weapons free zone. As a result of public pressure, more Members of Parliament will come onside in support of the intent and purpose of Bill C-678. I believe there will eventually be a majority of Members of Parliament who support what I and my Party are proposing today.
There are many Members of Parliament who are still undecided about the nuclear weapons issue and the most effective way to persuade those Members of Parliament, from a public point of view, is to pressure them to support a nuclear weapons free zone within Canada. As I indicated, it is important that we clean our own house before we begin to tell others how our world can be improved. While our world has great potential, its people face great uncertainty in the future largely because of the nuclear weapons issue.
I also want to say that I believe that unilateral disarmament is an unreasonable scenario, as far as I am concerned as an individual Member of Parliament. A multilateral agreement among all nations with nuclear capability is required to freeze the production of nuclear arms and eventually eliminate nuclear arms throughout the world. Until that happens there will continue to be a great deal of uncertainty about the future of our world. No one wants to face the prospect of another Hiroshima or Nagasaki or face the even greater destruction which is possible today with weapons which are hundreds and thousands of times more powerful than those of World War II.
I will conclude by asking all Members of Parliament to allow Bill C-678, an Act to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone, to move into committee where we can give it the very serious consideration that it needs. I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Dauphin for enabling me to bring this Bill to the House, and I would like to thank Members of Parliament for their co-operation earlier today. I ask for that co-operation in continuing to work toward a solution for this real and pressing problem which not only faces Canadians but the world.

Mr. Speaker, it has been a long and interesting afternoon so far. My own Bill is to be dealt with this afternoon and I doubt we will be able to deal with the third Bill on this short list.
I have some objections to the form of Bill C-678 which was brought before the House for the first time two days ago. It declares itself to be an Act to declare Canada a nuclear weapons free zone. That is something which this Party has favoured historically and which can be proven in the last 20 years of Hansard. It was approximately 20 years ago that the Conservative Government of Mr. Diefenbaker was defeated because of its position on keeping Canada a nuclear free zone.
If I may be forgiven for saying so, this Bill does show signs of being given hasty writing or editing. While it says that this Bill may be cited as the Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act, the explanatory note says that this Bill would declare Canada to be a nuclear weapons free nation. The Bill continues to discuss
March 30, 1983

such things as flight testing and the production of components therefor, which deals with many weapons. We are left somewhat puzzled as to exactly what this Bill entails.
Making Canada a weapons free zone is a fairly simple operation. I should first point out to those people who are not conversant with this subject that if Canada is made a nuclear weapons free zone, it in no way gives anyone any guarantee that other nations will respect that declaration and decide not to target us in case of a conflict. It does not mean that everyone in the world will say that they will not bomb Canada because it has declared itself a nuclear free zone. Otherwise, each of us would declare our own domiciles a nuclear free zone as well.
Back in 1979, an interesting development occurred. I was Minister of National Defence at that time and I stated that we would move the nuclear weapons that we had out of Canada by 1982. Having taken that position, which is so much in sympathy with the NDP position, they immediately voted us out of office to make sure it would not happen and put the Liberals back in. This was only history repeating itself. They did exactly the same thing in 1963, when Mr. Diefenbaker outlined his position clearly in the House of Commons. He had been to a NATO meeting in Nassau. He said:
I was in Nassau. I formed certain ideas. I read the communique that was issued there and I come to certain conclusions based on that communique. Those conclusions are as follows, and these are the views expressed also by the United States under secretary of state, George W. Ball: that nuclear war is indivisible; that there should be no further development of new nuclear power anywhere in the world; that nuclear weapons as a universal deterrent is a dangerous solution. Today an attempt is being made by the United States to have the NATO nations increase their conventional arms.
Mr. Diefenbaker went ahead with his speech in which he pointed out why they were not going to arm the Bomarc with nuclear warheads in Canada. At that time Mr. Pearson was the Liberal leader and his biographer, who is the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as we all know, pointed out that that great Liberal leader, Mr. Pearson had reversed his position entirely and taken a bunch of sheep with him. Going from direct opposition to nuclear weapons, he turned them into a Party supporting nuclear weapons in Canada. That night, after a speech by Mr. Tommy Douglas that I am sure he would not want to have repeated in the House, the NDP once again sided with the Liberals on nuclear weapons and voted the Conservatives out of office.
So the Conservative Party has nothing to be ashamed about in our position on nuclear weapons in Canada. We were in favour of not having them in Canada in 1963 and we lost the Government over that issue. We were in favour, in 1979, of a stated fixed date to get rid of the last of the nuclear weapons that the Liberals had brought to this country, and to have them out of here in 1982. It is now 1983, but thanks to the NDP support of the Liberal position in December, 1979 we were not allowed to go ahead with freeing this country from nuclear weapons.
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
Bearing that in mind, one looks with a certain amount of skepticism at this latest endeavour of the NDP to take no responsibility for their actions whatsoever, when they keep on bringing this militaristic, nuclear-favouring Government that we have at the present time into office and getting rid of the Conservatives who agree with them that we would like Canada to be a nuclear free nation.
I do not wish to belabour this point. One can be a little bit cynical about the approach that has been taken to date, but it is a very serious problem. The end that I trust we all wish to attain is to see a control of nuclear armaments not only in Canada but in nations throughout the world, and particularly among the superpowers. This Party would suggest to the Government that their first duty is to do everything in their power to approach both the U.S.S.R. and the Americans and persuade them to do their very best to find a way to have an agreement to de-escalate the arms race, to bring it to a stop, and then start reducing the number of nuclear weapons that are deployed in Europe particularly, but all over the world as well.
In line with this, the President of the United States today stated that he was making a new counteroffer, moving away from the zero/zero option that he had placed before the Russians more than a year ago to an offer that he would cut down the numbers of Cruise missiles and Pershing IIs that they intend to deploy in Europe, provided that the Russians would cut down their number of intermediate-range ballistic missiles that they have deployed anywhere in the world to an equal number.
One of the reasons that I wish to sit down before we hear the knock on the door for Royal Assent is that I would like to hear what the Liberal reaction is to this initiative by the President of the United States. The United States has responded to public pressure and to pressure from allies, and I think has taken a very reasonable and forward step to resolving the impasse that both of the protagonists have had for the last six months in not moving one millimetre from their original positions. Perhaps we could then have a more hopeful Easter.
Thank you for the time, Mr. Speaker, and it looks as if my Bill will be discussed a little later than expected this day.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rather than go into any partisan discussion on steps being taken to control nuclear weapons concentration, I would like to give the Government's position as it currently exists.
At the end of the World War II the Canadian Government decided not to develop its own nuclear weapons. Ours was the first country with the ability and means to do so which chose instead to devote all of its expertise to the peaceful uses of the atom. We are a member of an alliance which depends for its security on the nuclear deterrent. But the Canadian Forces do not have a nuclear role in NATO's forces in Europe. When the CF-18 is fully operational, replacing the Voodoo, the last nuclear warheads will be withdrawn from Canada.

March 30, 1983
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
Although Canada does not itself have a nuclear role either in Europe or, shortly, in North American defence, we are considering permitting the U.S.A. to test a weapons system, the Cruise missile, which can carry nuclear warheads. I would like to explain why.
In the 1970s the United States and the Soviet Union were involved in negotiating the SALT II agreement to limit at equal levels their strategic intercontinental nuclear weapons. At this point the Soviet Union began deploying a new intermediate-range missile into Europe, the SS-20, exceptionally accurate and carrying three nuclear warheads. With a range of
5,000	kilometres, it represented a potential threat to every city in Western Europe. Several Western European Governments feared that, by introducing a new, devastating missile for use in Europe, while it was codifying a balance in intercontinental weapons, the Soviet Union intended to threaten European NATO members and split the defence of Europe from the defence of North America. Chancellor Schmidt of West Germany first drew attention to the danger.
In December, 1979, at the request of the European members of the Alliance, NATO Ministers therefore took their two-track decision. They agreed to deploy 108 Pershing II launchers and 464 ground-launched Cruise missiles each with a single warhead to replace other shorter-range missiles, in order to balance the threat of the SS-20s. Secondly, they proposed negotiations between the Soviet Union and the United States to limit land-based intermediate-range missile systems on both sides.
The Soviet Union initially said it would not take part in the negotiations unless the deployment track was cancelled. However, it subsequently agreed to discussions and negotiations began in 1981. After consultations with its allies, the United States proposed the zero option, to abolish all land-based intermediate-range nuclear missiles on either side. This would clearly be the best result, because it would remove an entire category of weapon.
NATO has always made it clear that this is not a take it or leave it proposition. NATO members have repeatedly said that they are willing to consider any serious Soviet proposal. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told the House last week, we are not certain that the zero option is a realizeable goal. With other allies, Canada has urged the United States to look at a compromise or an intermediate solution, even though the ultimate goal of removing all of those weapons would remain. At the meeting of NATO defence ministers last week in Portugal, they listed the basic criteria for balanced and effective arms control: significant reductions based on equality of rights and limits between the United States and the Soviet Union, no inclusion of third party systems, global limitations so that Soviet missiles would not just be removed from Europe to Asia, no weakening of the USA contribution to NATO's conventional deterrence and defence, and effective verifiability.
Throughout the period of negotiations the Soviet Union has continued deploying SS-20 missiles. When NATO took its two-track decision in December 1979, the Soviet Union had
just over 100 SS-20s. Now it has 351, with over 1,000 warheads. These are in addition to over 250 older SS-4 and SS-5 missiles, which have enormous warheads in the megaton range, equal to a million tons of TNT. The Soviet Union has not yet made a serious proposal which would recognize the legitimate security interests of the West. On the contrary, the most recent Soviet proposal would actually leave them with more missiles than they had when the negotiations began, and allow the United States to deploy none.
On February 10, the Canadian Government concluded a framework agreement concerning the test and evaluation of U.S. defence systems in Canada. Under that agreement, specific test and evaluation proposals may be put forward by the U.S. Department of Defense for consideration by the Canadian Minister of National Defence or his representative. If approved, a project arrangement would be concluded between the U.S. Department of Defense and the Canadian Department of National Defence. Canada may refuse any proposal.
When the framework agreement was concluded, we were aware that Canada would likely be approached for a project arrangement to test the guidance system for the Cruise missile. Because this was expected, the framework agreement specified two restrictions on such testing. Cruise missiles shall be unarmed, and any flight corridors for such testing shall be selected to ensure minimum disruption to civil aviation operations and minimum disturbance to persons on the ground.
Ministers have made it clear that if Cruise missiles are tested, the testing would be linked intimately to Canada's security as a member of NATO and NORAD and to Canada's policy on arms control and disarmament. Successive Canadian governments have supported the NATO two-track decision, which called for the deployment of ground-launched Cruise missiles in Europe if the INF negotiations fail. We are convinced that the negotiations will not succeed if the Alliance shows signs of weakness. We cannot accept a result which would require NATO to abandon the modernization of its forces in Europe while the Soviet Union retains its force of SS-20 missiles intact.
Our European allies have volunteered to deploy new missiles on their soil, in order to provide an incentive for the Soviet Union to negotiate seriously in the intermediate-range nuclear force talks. NATO did not take the initiative in introducing this class of weapons into Europe. Its European members do not want ground-launched Cruise missiles or Pershing IIs for their own sakes, but they want Soviet SS-20 missiles aimed against them even less. They are convinced that the only way to persuade the Soviets to remove these or even reduce their numbers, is to prepare to deploy intermediate-range missiles on our side.
Canada will not be providing sites for the missiles. We expect merely to be asked to help with the testing of unarmed versions of the missiles. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)
March 30, 1983

has pointed out, we would be poor members of the Alliance if we said we would not even consider testing the guidance system of the missiles which our allies will be deploying in accordance with a NATO decision which Canada supported.
The United States has not yet formally approached the Government to conclude a Project Arrangement for testing Cruise missiles. Ministers have made it quite clear that Cabinet will have to consider such an arrangement carefully, and that no prior commitment has been given to the U.S.A. Government. In considering the issue, they have also made it clear, however, that one of the major considerations will be the need to support our allies in carrying out NATO's two-track decision.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are very conscious of the alarming number of nuclear weapons presently in the hands of the superpowers. They dread the thought that they might one day be used, and ponder over the dangers inherent in the existence of such arsenals. We are all aware of the devastation that would result from a nuclear war. In the face of the uncertainty that exists, many groups and individuals in the West are calling for an end to the development and deployment of new weapons, judging the quantity already in existence to be ample. This applies to strategic weapons as well as the intermediate-range missiles in Europe. Is it possible to accept the status quo in these two areas, and does it make sense to do so?
The governments of the NATO countries have decided to deploy Pershing II rockets and Cruise missiles in Europe as of this year if sufficient progress is not made in negotiations concerning this category of weapons in the coming months. It would have been much easier, in the short term, to pretend that the gigantic armament effort being made by the Warsaw Pact nations, in both the conventional and nuclear areas, was only a figment of our imagination. That is what the European countries did in the thirties. The imbalance that already existed in 1979, when NATO saw the need to react to the massive deployment of Soviet SS-20 missiles, has now become even greater, because the U.S.S.R. has since almost doubled the number of these missiles. Our allies are being held under a constant threat of destruction by more than 350 of these missiles, for which the West has no equivalent.
Canada has always been an advocate of peace, justice and freedom, but it must honour its commitments. The North Atlantic Alliance, of which Canada is a founding member, was formed to avoid a recurrence of war in Europe. Our soldiers who gave their lives for the liberation of Europe must not be said to have died in vain.
The Canadian Government, in accord with the other members of NATO, is very much in favour of verifiable agreements that would limit and then reduce nuclear weapons stocks on both sides, hopefully leading to eventual elimination. However, such an objective can only be achieved if the West shows its determination not to remain indifferent in the face of what
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
might constitute a means of applying considerable pressure. History has demonstrated that it is impossible to bring about a substantial diminution of armaments when the forces of one side outweigh the other's, as is presently the case in Europe. What reason would the side with the greater forces have to destroy or to dismantle the weapons that give it its hard-earned advantage, when no similar reduction had to be made by the other? Aggression is fostered by a state of inequality and a lack of determination, with the appearance of weakness.
Our policy is not one of confrontation. On the contrary, it is the only way open to us in the slow process of nuclear arms limitation and disarmament. It is based on the concept of deterrence, which has given us a hitherto unequalled period of almost 40 years without a major conflict in this region of Europe where military forces of unprecedented size are facing each other. And this is where the real merit of mutual deterrence lies. There can be no recourse to atomic weapons, because the superpowers have the capacity to resist a preemptive strike and to inflict on the aggressor a degree of destruction that would obviate the political acceptability of initiating a strike. Nor has there been any use of conventional weapons, which over the two World Wars alone were responsible for tens of millions of deaths and so much destruction.
There were more victims in the bombardment of Tokyo on March 9, 1945 than at Hiroshima; 83,600 deaths and 102,000 wounded, compared with 80,000 deaths and 70,000 wounded at Hiroshima. That is no exoneration of the travesty that happened at Hiroshima. We all hope and pray that that will never be repeated. It will not be repeated if one side, the West, shows weakness in fight in the face of Soviet might. This is the result of the state of mutual deterrence that has gradually established itself between the superpowers and opposing alliances.
The strategy of non-war and non-use of forces can exist only in so far as the fragile equilibrium is maintained. There exists a moral obligation to keep intact the state of deterrence and to negotiate in good faith nuclear and conventional arms control agreements which are balanced and verifiable and which will reduce the arsenals of both sides to the lowest possible level. It is my hope, Mr. Speaker, that both sides in this very important issue, this issue upon which the very survival of our world depends, will in fact be responsible, so that neither side will proceed to the development of any further new weapons, but will put all of their resources which they are now expending on the development of new weapons into the development of a means of peace, the development of a means of reduction of arms, and the development of the means to achieve a world where men and women and future generations can live without the fear of a nuclear holocaust and can have a reasonable hope that the world, as we know it, will survive. We will then be able to truly progress and leave the world a better place for future generations.

March 30, 1983
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention at this time to follow up on the comments of the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) which he made on behalf of the Government.
The primary objective of any arms control and disarmament initiative, including the concept of a nuclear weapons free zone, is to enhance security. The control and reduction of armaments, particularly nuclear armaments, can constitute an integral component of Canada's security policy. The Speech from The Throne at the opening of Parliament in 1980 outlined Canada's balanced and coherent security policy. The Government expressed its commitment to do its full part in increasing the military capability of the North Atlantic Alliance, to provide security for its members, and its dedication to active cooperation in efforts to achieve international agreements on equitable and verifiable arms control and disarmament measures.
For many years Canada's security position has been based on these two essential and complimentary elements. We have sought, through the vigorous and determined pursuit of arms control and disarmament agreements, to reduce the risk of global conflict and nuclear war inherent in a situation where a nation or groups of nations face each other with large and destructive arsenals. We have done this because any such war would not only threaten the survival of all Canadians, given the destructiveness of nuclear weapons, it would destroy most of our civilization. As stated in the 1980 Throne Speech:
Canada's imperative is clear. This Government must continue its strategy to suffocate the deadly growth in the nuclear arsenals of the world. We must, and we will, actively cooperate in international efforts to negotiate agreements on
March 30, 1983

verifiable means of arms control and disarmament, and seek to rally others to a cause that is no less than human survival on this planet.
But we have to recognize that nations will not lightly give up the security which military strength and modern weapons provide them. For this reason arms control and disarmament agreements cannot be ends in themselves; their objective is to enhance security at a lower level of armaments. Nor can they be achieved easily and quickly. Acceptable and workable arms control and disarmament formulae are not found in the course of negotiations in which one of the parties is at a significant disadvantage vis-a-vis the other in military power. It is for this reason that the other element of Canadian security policy has required close and, in recent years, increasingly urgent attention. This is in the maintenance of adequate forces to protect Canada by contributing to the collective deterrence and defence capacity of the North Atlantic Alliance.
We are determined to do what we can by negotiation to ameliorate the international security environment, mindful always that it will be a long and difficult task and that we must tread warily. We have no choice but to make the effort. The future of our civilization may be at stake. We have therefore tried, and will go on trying, in conjunction with our friends and allies, to prevent an escalation of the nuclear arms race.
Three Canadian priorities in the nuclear arms control and disarmament field are: to support strongly negotiations to limit and reduce nuclear arms; to promote early progress toward the realization of a multilateral comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty; and to promote the evolution of an effective nuclear non-proliferation regime based on the Non-Proliferation Treaty. The Government has attached particular importance to the implementation of Article VI of the NPT, which commits all parties to pursue negotiations in good faith toward the cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date, nuclear disarmament and a treaty on general and complete disarmament.
Canada continues to pursue these priorities in appropriate international forums and in bilateral negotiations. The Government takes every opportunity to stress the importance it attaches to the negotiations to limit and reduce nuclear arms. We will continue to promote, through consultations with our allies, progress in the START and INF negotiations intended to limit and reduce inventories of both strategic and intermediate-range nuclear weapons.
The priority which Canada continues to attach to the limitation and reduction of nuclear forces and to progress toward a comprehensive test ban reflects the complementary dual approach which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) set out in his address to UNSSOD II last year. On the one hand, this approach would include progress to implement the strategy of suffocation through agreements designed to inhibit the development of new weapons systems. A comprehensive test ban treaty would be one of the main elements. This approach would be complemented by active pursuit of agreements on qualitative and quantitative reductions in nuclear arsenals
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
through the INF and START talks to achieve a stable nuclear balance at lower levels.
The strategy of suffocation is being actively promoted in international forums, in particular at the United Nations. Moreover, we continue to contribute concretely to more specific discussions which deal with implementing elements of the strategy. Canada has called for the resumption of the U.K./U.S.A./U.S.S.R. talks on a comprehensive test ban. In the Committee on Disarmament in Geneva, we are actively participating in the work toward the realization of a nuclear test ban agreement and in the efforts of the Seismic Experts Group, which is developing an international verification system for an eventual test ban treaty. We have also continued our efforts to effect implementation of the second and third elements of the strategy. Although we are also doing our utmost with regard to the fourth element, agreements to reduce military budgets cannot be concluded until the U.S.S.R. assumes a more open policy with regard to information about its military spending.
As a strong supporter of the non-proliferation treaty, Canada is fully committed to preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. The non-proliferation treaty also requires the sharing of knowledge regarding the peaceful use of nuclear technology, particularly to the energy-poor countries of the world. Canada is also fully committed to doing this, but only if the transfer of such nuclear technology is properly and adequately safeguarded. Canada's non-proliferation safeguards policy has been developed to ensure that our nuclear exports do not contribute to nuclear weapons proliferation.
All Candu reactors are fully safeguarded, and operate under strict international controls supervised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Indeed, Canadian safeguards are more comprehensive than those demanded by competing nuclear suppliers. Despite suggestions that these measures are too restrictive, the Government of Canada has consistently resisted pressure to downgrade its requirements.
It should furthermore be understood that nuclear reactors are by no means synonymous with nuclear weapons. Candu reactor technology is designed exclusively for the generation of electrical power. To produce weapons grade materials, the spent reactor fuel must be reprocessed to extract plutonium. This process is technically sophisticated, enormously expensive, difficult to conceal and strictly regulated internationally. In the contemporary situation it is unlikely that sufficient quantities of plutonium could be diverted, reprocessed and a nuclear device constructed without these actions being detected by international authorities. Accordingly, the sale of Candu reactors abroad cannot be equated with the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
Consistent with our non-proliferation policy, Canada has been strongly sympathetic, in principle, to the concept of nuclear weapon-free zones where they command the support of the countries in the area and promote regional and international stability. While we have not considered such zones to be a fully satisfactory alternative to the ratification of the nonproliferation treaty by the countries of the areas concerned, we

March 30, 1983
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone
do believe that, in the absence of universal or near universal adherence to the non-proliferation treaty and provided certain principles are observed, the creation of such zones can make a significant contribution to the objective of preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. Canada has supported United Nations resolutions calling for such zones in Africa, the Middle East and south Asia. We have also backed measures which would consolidate the establishment of a nuclear weapons free zone in Latin America in accordance with the Treaty of Tlatelolco, in spite of Canadian opposition to a provision in the treaty which allows for the explosion of nuclear devices for so-called peaceful purposes.
We believe that, to be effective, such zones must apply to a well-defined geographic area; be based on proposals which emanate from and are agreed to by most countries in the area concerned, including the principal military powers of the area; not give military advantage to any state or group of states; contain adequate treaty assurances and means to verify that all countries abide by the commitment involved; and not permit countries of the area to have independent nuclear explosive capability.
As stated above, the objective of any arms control and disarmament initiative, including the concept of a nuclear weapon-free zone, is to enhance security. The Canadian Government continues to believe in the concept of mutual security-a collective effort to deter aggression or to counter it if it occurs. That is why we are in the North Atlantic Alliance, which is also the framework for the NORAD agreement with the USA. The Alliance relies on a deterrent strategy in which nuclear weapons play an important part. This is unfortunately unavoidable in the world as we know it. The idea of a nuclear weapon-free zone for Canada would be realistic only if the Canadian Government were prepared to withdraw from the Alliance which has served us well and has helped to preserve peace for more than thirty years. The Canadian Government continues to believe that our defence partnership, cooperation and defence production sharing arrangements with our allies make a greater contribution to preserving peace and security than would our withdrawal into the isolation of a nuclear weapon-free zone.
In order to rationalize the defence production arrangements which we undertake in support of our collective security commitments, Canada has, since 1959, participated in Defence Development and Production Sharing Arrangements with the United States and our other Alliance partners. These were undertaken by the government of the day in recognition of the fact that Canada could not continue funding the development of complex and high cost aerospace and electronic systems for the small domestic market.
The decision to develop certain limited sectors of Canadian expertise has proven highly successful. The Canadian defence industry has established itself as a competitive producer of such diverse products as short take-off and landing aircraft,
STOL, airborne reconnaissance vehicles, radio communications and flight simulators. The dual military-civilian application of such technology has allowed Canada to become a major competitor in both markets.
Given that such development and production sharing arrangements put Canadian firms in direct competition with well-established foreign manufacturers, often supported by Government subsidies and military procurement programs much greater than those of Canada, the Government of Canada has provided domestic firms with financing assistance to compensate for these disadvantages. The eligibility criteria of this program were expanded in 1968 to include civilian aerospace and avionics projects in recognition of the spill-over from military technology and Canada's increased ability to penetrate this broader market. In recent years this program has increasingly emphasized more profitable civilian production in order to enhance the return to Canadians on their investment.
Litton Systems of Canada Limited was awarded a subcontract by the United States Department of Defence through its parent company in the United States, Litton Industries, to produce a portion of the inertial guidance systems for the Cruise missile. Such production comes under the Canadian-American defence production sharing arrangement and as such is eligible for and has received financial assistance from the Government of Canada. Litton's participation in a small part of the Cruise missile vehicle program should not be taken as a change in Canadian policies instituted at the end of the 1960s to divest our Armed Forces of a nuclear weapon role. However, it is consistent with our joint defence efforts with our NATO allies who rely in part, as we do, on the maintenance of a credible nuclear deterrent against attack from hostile states.
Finally, as is well known, the only nuclear weapons in Canada are the United States air-to-air missiles which enable the CF-101 to play an effective role in the defence of North America. When the CF-18A have replaced the CF-101, this role will be carried out with conventional weapons and therefore there will no longer be a requirement for these nuclear weapons to be held in Canada.
